newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hughes' Armstrong says not in talks on AT&T post.
newsitem.headline: Hughes' Armstrong says not in talks on AT&T post.

text.p: Michael Armstrong, the Hughes Electronics Corp. executive reported to be a candidate to take over as president of AT&T Corp., said Wednesday he intends to stay in his present job.
Armstrong flatly denied U.S. media speculation that he would be picked as president of the long-distance carrier this week.
"It is just not true that I am in discussions with AT&T. I haven't been contacted by the company and I haven't been offered the job," Armstrong, in Tokyo on Hughes business, told Reuters.
"I am very happy and intend to stay with Hughes ... because it's a fantastic company," he said.
Asked if he would take the AT&T job if it were offered, he said: "I haven't the faintest idea."

Alex Mandl, who had been touted as a likely successor to AT&T Chairman Robert Allen, abruptly resigned as AT&T president and chief operating officer in August to head a small wireless communications company.
Armstrong, who has successfully restructured Hughes into a consumer electronics company from a defence contractor, was mentioned in U.S. media last week as the leading candidate for the job.
Armstrong also denied market talk that Hughes hoped to become independent of its biggest shareholder, General Motors Corp.
"It used to be true. Because we needed to have a greater liquidity or stock, we were hopeful to get a more knowledgeable governance of our company," he said.

But from Hughes' perspective "the problem was solved," Armstrong said. Over the past four years, Hughes had increased its liquidity and now has its own board of directors with greater delegated authority, he said.
"The GM board has been very supportive of all of our investments as we diversified the company and have gone much more heavily in telecommunications," Armstrong said.

Wall Street has speculated that GM may want to spin off Hughes, which the carmaker acquired in 1985 for more than $5 billion. Analysts have said that the rapidly changing Hughes no longer fits in GM's mix of business.

Armstrong, who left for the United States later Wednesday, was in Tokyo to announce that DirecTV Japan Inc., a Hughes subsidiary, would start a digital satellite broadcasting service in Japan in the fall of 1997.
He did not rule out the possibility that DirecTV might link up with Japanese broadcasters, saying "all options are available to us."
